title: Null safety mind map
intro: Null in C# is two stories told with the same `?` symbol. On value types like `int`, the question mark wraps the value in a real struct (`Nullable<T>`). On reference types like `string`, it is a compiler annotation that warns you before run time — but null references still exist at run time. This module teaches both machines, how to enable nullable reference types (NRT), when to use runtime guards instead of the null-forgiving operator `!`, and how this compares to TypeScript strictNullChecks.

conceptCards.title: Value vs reference ?
conceptCards.summary: int? is System.Nullable<int> at run time. string? is still System.String — the ? is a compiler annotation.
conceptCards.example: int? score = null; // HasValue is false

conceptCards.title: NRT annotations
conceptCards.summary: Enable <Nullable>enable</Nullable>. Annotate string vs string?. Compiler warns on CS8600-family mismatches.

conceptCards.title: Guards vs !
conceptCards.summary: ThrowIfNull throws and updates null-state. x! only suppresses warnings — zero run-time effect.

conceptCards.title: required and attributes
conceptCards.summary: required forces initialization, not non-null. MaybeNull and NotNullWhen teach generic Try* contracts.

conceptCards.title: NRT vs strictNullChecks
conceptCards.summary: Both are compile-time. C# adds Nullable<T> struct and NullReferenceException. JSON and Redis are still untyped.
conceptCards.example: Deserialize<T>()! // same trust class as JSON.parse + as T
